### Question 67 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** git diff only reports differences; git cherry-pick actually replays the selected commits onto the current branch, producing new commits that replicate the original changes.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** git diff computes a patch between the two branch tips, and applying that patch will automatically create new commits on the target branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is incorrect. git diff only generates a textual representation of the changes; it does not automatically create commits. To turn a diff into a commit you would need to apply the patch manually and then run git commit, which is a separate step.

**Option:** git cherry-pick displays a line‑by‑line comparison of the changes introduced by each commit without modifying any branches. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is wrong. git cherry-pick does not merely display differences; it re‑applies the selected commit(s) onto the current HEAD, thereby altering history. Its purpose is to copy code changes, not to provide a read‑only diff view.

**Option:** git diff shows the differences between the branches but does not change any history, while git cherry-pick copies the selected commits onto the current branch, preserving the original commit IDs. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This answer is inaccurate. While it correctly notes that git diff is non‑destructive, it falsely claims that cherry‑pick preserves the original commit IDs. In reality cherry‑pick creates new commit objects with new SHA‑1 hashes, even though the content is the same.

**Option:** git diff only reports differences; git cherry-pick actually replays the selected commits onto the current branch, producing new commits that replicate the original changes. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is correct. git diff is a read‑only operation that shows what changed between two points, whereas git cherry‑pick takes specific commits from another branch and applies them as new commits on the current branch. The new commits get their own identifiers, which is why cherry‑pick is used for selective integration of work.

**Option:** git cherry-pick merges the entire source branch into the destination, preserving the original commit IDs. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is false. cherry‑pick works on individual commits, not on the whole branch, and it does not preserve the original IDs. To merge an entire branch you would use git merge or git rebase, not cherry‑pick.

**Option:** git diff can be used to permanently rewrite the target branch to match the source branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This claim is incorrect. git diff only shows differences; it never alters any branch. To rewrite a branch you would use commands like git reset, git revert, or git merge, but not git diff.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of the functional distinction between a comparison tool (git diff) and a commit‑replaying tool (git cherry-pick). git diff provides a read‑only view of changes between two commits or branches and never modifies the repository, making it suitable for code review or generating patches. git cherry-pick, on the other hand, actively applies chosen commits onto the current HEAD, creating new commit objects with new SHA‑1 hashes, which is useful for selective back‑porting or feature integration. Common misconceptions include believing that diff can create commits automatically or that cherry-pick merely shows changes without affecting history; both are inaccurate. Best practice is to use git diff when you need to inspect or generate patches, and use git cherry-pick when you want to incorporate specific changes without merging the whole branch.

[Back to Question](#question-67)

### Question 68 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Run git revert <commit SHA> on the feature branch and commit the resulting revert.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Run git reset --hard <commit> and force‑push the branch to origin. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because git reset --hard rewrites the branch history by moving the branch pointer to an older commit. Force‑pushing a rewritten history can disrupt teammates who have already based work on the existing commits. It also discards any later commits, which is far more destructive than simply undoing a single change.

**Option:** Use git checkout <commit> to detach HEAD, make changes, and push the detached state. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is incorrect; checking out a specific commit creates a detached HEAD state that is not attached to any branch. Pushing from a detached HEAD is not supported and would create a new anonymous branch, leaving the original feature branch unchanged. Therefore it does not revert the unwanted commit on the intended branch.

**Option:** Run git revert <commit SHA> on the feature branch and commit the resulting revert. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This is the correct approach. git revert creates a new commit that inverses the changes introduced by the specified commit, preserving the existing commit history. It is safe for shared branches because it does not rewrite history, and collaborators can pull the revert without conflict.

**Option:** Amend the original commit with git commit --amend to remove the unwanted changes. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Amending only works on the most recent commit and only if it has not been pushed to a shared repository. Since the commit was made by another developer and is likely not the tip of the branch, git commit --amend cannot modify it. Attempting this would either fail or create a new history that conflicts with collaborators.

**Option:** Rebase interactively (git rebase -i) and drop the specific commit from the branch history. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While interactive rebase can remove a commit, it rewrites the branch history, which is dangerous on a branch that others may have pulled. Dropping the commit would require force‑pushing and could cause merge conflicts for anyone who has based work on the original history. Therefore it is not the most appropriate method for a simple revert.

**Option:** Delete the feature branch, recreate it from the main branch, and cherry‑pick the desired commits. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Deleting and recreating the branch is an extreme measure that discards all work on the branch, not just the unwanted commit. Cherry‑picking each needed commit is time‑consuming and error‑prone, and the original branch context is lost. This approach is unnecessary when a single revert commit can achieve the goal.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of how to safely undo a specific change in a collaborative Git environment. The correct action is to use git revert, which adds a new commit that undoes the effects of the targeted commit while preserving the linear history, making it safe for shared branches. Common misconceptions include thinking that resetting or force‑pushing is acceptable, even though those actions rewrite history and can disrupt teammates. Amend and interactive rebase are also often suggested, but they only work for recent or unshared commits and otherwise require history rewriting. Best practice is to choose the least disruptive method—git revert—for reverting public commits, and to avoid any operation that alters existing published history.

### Question 69 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answers:**
- Perform an interactive rebase of each feature branch onto the main branch, resolving conflicts as they arise.
- Create a dedicated integration branch, merge all feature branches into it, resolve the conflicts there, and then merge the integration branch back to main.
- Use `git cherry-pick` to selectively apply commits from one branch to another, handling conflicts individually.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Perform an interactive rebase of each feature branch onto the main branch, resolving conflicts as they arise. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. An interactive rebase rewrites the feature branch history so that its commits are applied on top of the current main branch, giving you the opportunity to resolve conflicts commit‑by‑commit. By handling each conflict during the rebase, you maintain a clean linear history, which simplifies future merges and makes the Git log easier to understand.

**Option:** Merge the feature branches directly into the main branch and let Git resolve the conflicts automatically. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Merging without first inspecting the changes can produce large, ambiguous merge commits where Git may choose one side arbitrarily, potentially discarding important logic. In real projects this often leads to subtle bugs that are hard to trace back to the original conflicting change.

**Option:** Create a dedicated integration branch, merge all feature branches into it, resolve the conflicts there, and then merge the integration branch back to main. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. An integration branch acts as a sandbox where you can combine multiple feature branches, address all conflicts in one place, and run integration tests before affecting the main line. Once the integration branch is clean, merging it back into main introduces a single, well‑tested commit that represents the resolved state.

**Option:** Use `git cherry-pick` to selectively apply commits from one branch to another, handling conflicts individually. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Cherry‑picking lets you pick specific changes that you know are safe while leaving problematic commits out, giving fine‑grained control over conflict resolution. After resolving each cherry‑picked conflict, you can commit the changes, ensuring that only the desired functionality makes its way into the target branch.

**Option:** Delete the conflicting branches and recreate them from the main branch to avoid the conflicts entirely. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Deleting and recreating branches discards the work that caused the conflict, which may include valuable features or bug fixes. Rather than solving the conflict, it forces you to re‑implement the changes, increasing technical debt and risking loss of context.

**Option:** Force‑push the resolved state to the remote repository without notifying teammates, bypassing any review process. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Force‑pushing overwrites shared history, which can disrupt collaborators' work and lead to lost commits or merge errors on their local clones. Proper conflict resolution should be communicated and, ideally, reviewed through pull requests to maintain team alignment and code quality.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests a candidate's understanding of reliable strategies for reconciling divergent feature branches in a collaborative environment. Interactive rebasing, using an integration branch, and cherry‑picking are all proven techniques that give developers explicit control over conflicts while preserving useful history and enabling thorough testing. Merging without inspection, deleting branches, or force‑pushing bypass essential review and integration steps, often resulting in hidden bugs, lost work, or coordination breakdowns. In practice, teams should choose the method that best fits their workflow—rebasing for linear history, integration branches for large feature sets, and cherry‑picking for selective changes—while always communicating resolutions to teammates. Following these best practices ensures a stable codebase and smooth collaboration across multiple feature streams.

### Question 70 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Your local branch contains commits that are not present on the remote, causing the histories to diverge.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Your local branch is missing the remote's latest commits, so you need to pull first. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is incorrect. A non‑fast‑forward error occurs when the local branch has commits that are not on the remote, not when it is simply missing remote commits. If you were only missing remote changes, a normal fast‑forward merge or pull would succeed without error.

**Option:** You attempted to push after using git reset --hard to a previous commit, discarding remote history. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While resetting to an older commit can lead to a non‑fast‑forward situation, the root cause of the error is still the presence of divergent commits. The reset itself is not the cause; it is the fact that the local branch now lacks commits that exist on the remote. The error alerts you that pushing would overwrite remote history.

**Option:** Your remote repository is configured as a mirror, which rejects non‑fast‑forward updates. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is a misunderstanding. Mirror repositories do reject non‑fast‑forward pushes, but they are a special server‑side configuration and not the typical reason developers see this error in day‑to‑day work. Most developers encounter the error because of divergent commit histories, not because the remote is a mirror.

**Option:** Your local branch contains commits that are not present on the remote, causing the histories to diverge. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This is the correct answer. A non‑fast‑forward error is raised when the local branch has commits that the remote does not, meaning Git cannot simply move the remote tip forward. In practice, you must either pull and merge/rebase the remote changes or force‑push if you truly intend to overwrite the remote history.

**Option:** Git is preventing you because the branch you are working on is protected by branch protection rules. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Branch protection rules can block force pushes, but they do not generate a non‑fast‑forward error; instead, Git Hub returns a permission‑denied message. The error described is specifically about history divergence, not about permission settings. Therefore this option is not the root cause of the non‑fast‑forward situation.

**Option:** The remote's HEAD points to a different branch, so Git cannot fast‑forward. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is inaccurate. The remote's HEAD reference simply indicates the default branch and does not affect push operations on a specific branch. A non‑fast‑forward error is unrelated to which branch HEAD points to; it strictly concerns divergent commit histories on the same branch.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of why Git reports a non‑fast‑forward error when attempting to synchronize a local branch with its remote counterpart. The core concept is that Git can only fast‑forward a branch when the remote tip is a direct descendant of the local tip; otherwise, the histories have diverged. The correct answer points out that the local branch has unique commits not present on the remote, which is the most common scenario causing this error. Common misconceptions include believing the error stems from missing remote commits, protected branches, or server configurations, but those either produce different messages or are less frequent. Best practice is to examine the commit graph with commands like git log --oneline --graph and then either pull/rebase to integrate remote changes or, if appropriate, use a forced push with caution.

[Back to Question](#question-70)

### Question 71 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answers:**
- Run `git revert <commit-hash>` and then push the new revert commit to the remote.
- Use `git reset --hard <commit-hash>` to move the branch pointer back and then force‑push (`git push --force`) to overwrite the remote history.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Run `git revert <commit-hash>` and then push the new revert commit to the remote. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. `git revert` creates a new commit that undoes the changes introduced by the specified commit without altering existing history. Because it adds a commit, the push proceeds normally and collaborators' histories remain intact, making it the safest choice for public branches.

**Option:** Use `git reset --hard <commit-hash>` to move the branch pointer back and then force‑push (`git push --force`) to overwrite the remote history. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is also correct, though it rewrites history. `git reset --hard` discards commits after the chosen one, and a forced push replaces the remote branch with the rewritten local branch. It should only be used when you have agreement from the team and the branch is not shared with unmerged work, because other developers will have to reconcile the rewritten history.

**Option:** Execute `git commit --amend` to modify the unwanted commit and then push. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. `git commit --amend` only changes the most recent commit, and after a push it still requires a forced push to replace the remote commit. It cannot be used to amend an older commit without an interactive rebase, and using it on a shared branch can cause history divergence.

**Option:** Checkout the unwanted commit into a new branch and delete the original branch on the remote. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Checking out a previous commit creates a detached HEAD or a new branch, but it does not modify the existing remote branch. Deleting the original remote branch would also delete any other commits that were valid, potentially causing loss of work for the team.

**Option:** Use `git rebase -i` to drop the unwanted commit, then push normally. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. An interactive rebase that removes a commit rewrites the branch's history, so a normal `git push` will be rejected by the remote because it is non‑fast‑forward. To apply the rebased branch you would need to force‑push, which the answer does not mention, making the statement incomplete and misleading.

**Option:** Run `git reset --soft <commit-hash>` and then create a new commit that omits the changes. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A soft reset leaves the changes from the discarded commits staged, requiring additional manual editing and a new commit. Moreover, the branch history has still been rewritten, so you would need to force‑push to update the remote. It is more complex and error‑prone than the recommended revert or hard‑reset approaches.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of how to undo a commit that has already been shared on a remote branch. The safest, non‑destructive method is `git revert`, which adds a new commit that neutralizes the unwanted changes while preserving the existing commit history, so a regular push suffices. When a team agrees to rewrite history, `git reset --hard` followed by a forced push can also be used, but it overwrites the remote and requires careful coordination to avoid disrupting collaborators. Common misconceptions include thinking `git commit --amend` works for any past commit, believing a regular push will succeed after a rebase without force, or assuming checking out an old commit automatically fixes the remote branch. Best practice is to prefer `git revert` for public branches and reserve history‑rewriting techniques for private or tightly controlled branches, always communicating with teammates before forcing changes.

[Back to Question](#question-71)

### Question 72 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Stash the changes using git stash.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Commit the changes to the current branch before switching. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is not the best first step. While committing preserves your work, it creates a permanent history entry for potentially incomplete or experimental changes, which may not be desired. In a real QA workflow, you might want to keep the work transient until you have verified the feature, and committing could clutter the branch with noisy commits.

**Option:** Discard the changes with git reset --hard. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Discarding changes outright is incorrect because it permanently deletes any modifications you have made, causing loss of effort. This command is useful when you intentionally want to revert to the last committed state, but not when you need to preserve work. Using it here would force you to recreate the changes from scratch, wasting time and potentially introducing errors.

**Option:** Stash the changes using git stash. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** Stashing is the correct first action. The git stash command saves your uncommitted changes on a stack, allowing you to switch branches safely without losing work. Later you can reapply the stash with git stash pop, preserving the original context and keeping the commit history clean.

**Option:** Force the branch switch with git checkout -f. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Forcing a checkout bypasses safety checks and discards any local modifications, which defeats the purpose of preserving your work. The -f flag tells Git to throw away changes, leading to potential data loss. It is only appropriate when you deliberately want to ignore and delete those changes, not in this scenario.

**Option:** Create a new temporary branch and commit the changes there before switching. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Creating a new temporary branch adds unnecessary complexity as a first step. While committing on a new branch would retain the changes, it requires additional Git operations (branch creation, checkout, commit) that are not needed just to safeguard current edits. The simpler stash approach achieves the same protection with fewer steps.

**Option:** Pull the latest changes from the remote repository before switching branches. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Pulling updates has no relevance to protecting your local uncommitted changes. It synchronizes the current branch with its remote counterpart but does not address the risk of losing work when changing branches. Executing a pull first would waste time and might even introduce merge conflicts that are unrelated to the original problem.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests the learner's understanding of how to safely move between branches when there are uncommitted modifications. Git stash is the canonical solution because it temporarily saves those changes without committing them, enabling a clean branch checkout. Common misconceptions include thinking that committing first is always safest, or that forcing a checkout will preserve work, both of which either pollute history or discard changes. Creating extra branches or pulling remote updates are extra steps that do not directly protect local edits. Best practice is to stash (or optionally commit) any work-in-progress before switching branches, then apply or pop the stash when you return, ensuring no loss of effort and a tidy repository history.

[Back to Question](#question-72)

### Question 73 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Create the branch locally and immediately push it to a remote repository, setting the upstream with `git push -u origin <branch-name>`.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Create the branch locally and immediately push it to a remote repository, setting the upstream with `git push -u origin <branch-name>`. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This is correct because pushing the branch to a remote stores the commits outside the local repository. As long as the remote reference exists, deleting the local branch does not remove the work; it can be recovered by fetching the remote branch. In practice, teams use this pattern to back up feature work and enable collaborative development.

**Option:** Enable the `branch. autosetuprebase=always` configuration so that the new branch automatically rebases onto the main branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is incorrect. The `branch. autosetuprebase` setting only influences how new branches are created with respect to rebasing, not how they are persisted or protected. It does not create any backup on a remote and therefore does not prevent loss if the branch is deleted. Misunderstanding this option can lead developers to think rebasing safeguards their work, which it does not.

**Option:** Configure `git gc. prune Expire` to "now" so that unreachable commits are retained indefinitely. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is incorrect. Setting `gc. prune Expire` to "now" actually makes Git prune unreachable objects immediately, which increases the risk of losing commits, not protecting them. The option deals with garbage collection, not with ensuring branch existence. Relying on this would be disastrous for preserving work.

**Option:** Use `git stash` to save the changes before deleting the branch, and configure `stash. save` to persist the stash across deletions. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is incorrect. While `git stash` can temporarily store uncommitted changes, it is not a configuration that guarantees persistence after a branch is deleted, especially if the stash is not pushed to a remote. Stashing is meant for short‑term context switching, not long‑term backup of a feature branch.

**Option:** Set the repository to be a bare repository by configuring `core. bare=true`. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is incorrect. A bare repository does not have a working directory and is typically used as a central remote, but simply making a repository bare does not automatically protect a specific branch from deletion. Without explicitly pushing the branch to a remote bare repo, the work could still be lost. This misconception confuses repository type with branch safety mechanisms.

**Option:** Configure `branch.<branch-name>. merge` to point to `refs/heads/main` so the feature branch always merges into main automatically. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This is incorrect. The `branch.<name>. merge` setting only tells Git which upstream branch to merge with, it does not create a backup or prevent deletion of the feature branch. Developers might think that linking to main preserves the work, but the branch can still be removed and its commits would be lost if not pushed elsewhere.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of how to preserve feature work beyond the lifetime of a local branch. The reliable way to avoid losing changes when a branch is deleted is to push the branch to a remote repository and set an upstream reference, which creates a durable copy that can be fetched later. Many learners mistakenly believe that local configuration options like rebasing, garbage‑collection settings, or stashing can provide the same safety, but those options either affect commit history handling or only offer temporary storage. Branch protection rules on the remote can further prevent accidental deletion, reinforcing best practice of always pushing feature branches. Remember to regularly push and verify remote branches to keep work safe and enable collaboration.

[Back to Question](#question-73)

### Question 74 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Push the new feature branch to a remote repository before deleting the local branch.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Merge the feature branch into the main branch before deleting the feature branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because merging the branch into main permanently integrates the changes, which may not be desired if the feature is still under development or needs further review. Merging too early can introduce unfinished code into the production line, potentially causing regressions. The engineer's goal is to preserve the work without necessarily merging it, so this does not address the safety of the isolated changes.

**Option:** Create a lightweight tag on the branch's tip and push the tag to the remote repository. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While tagging does create a permanent reference to a commit, this option is not the most straightforward way to ensure a feature branch is safe from deletion. Tags are typically used for releases or specific milestones, not for ongoing development work. Moreover, the engineer would still need to remember to push the tag and manage it separately, making this a less common practice for protecting a feature branch.

**Option:** Stash the changes before deleting the branch, assuming the stash will keep them safe. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Stashing is a temporary storage mechanism for uncommitted changes; it does not protect committed work on a branch. If the engineer has already committed the changes, stashing adds no benefit, and even for uncommitted work, a stash can be lost if mishandled or if the repository is cloned elsewhere. Therefore, relying on stash does not guarantee the changes will survive branch deletion.

**Option:** Push the new feature branch to a remote repository before deleting the local branch. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This statement is correct because pushing the branch to a remote creates a durable reference that survives local deletions. The remote repository retains all commits, and the branch can be fetched or recreated at any time, ensuring no loss of work. This is the standard best practice for safeguarding feature work when cleaning up local branches.

**Option:** Delete the local branch and rely on Git's reflog to recover the commits later if needed. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Although reflog can sometimes help locate dangling commits, it is not a reliable safety net; reflog entries can expire, and they are not shared with the remote. Relying on reflog assumes the user will remember the exact commit hashes and that the reflog has not been pruned, which is risky for important feature work. Hence, this approach does not guarantee the changes will be preserved.

**Option:** Use git revert to undo the changes before deleting the branch, thinking this will keep a record of the work. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Git revert creates new commits that reverse the changes, effectively discarding the original work rather than preserving it. This approach loses the original development history and does not protect the branch itself. Therefore, it does not meet the requirement of keeping the feature changes safe should the branch be deleted.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of how Git references protect work. Branches are merely pointers to commits; deleting a branch removes the pointer but not the commits themselves as long as another reference (e. g., another branch, tag, or remote) points to them. Pushing a branch to a remote creates such a persistent reference, making the work recoverable even after local deletion. Common misconceptions include thinking that merging, stashing, tagging, reflog, or revert provide the same safety, but each either alters the commit history, offers only temporary storage, or is unreliable for long‑term preservation. Best practice is to push feature branches to a remote early and often, ensuring a backup exists before any local cleanup.

[Back to Question](#question-74)

### Question 75 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Cherry-pick the specific commit from main onto the feature branch using `git cherry-pick <commit‑sha>`.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Merge the main branch into the feature branch with `git merge main`. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect for the stated need. A merge brings the entire history of the main branch into the feature branch, not just a single commit. Using merge would introduce unrelated changes and potentially create a larger integration effort than necessary, which contradicts the requirement to apply only one specific commit.

**Option:** Rebase the feature branch onto main using `git rebase main`. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Rebasing rewrites the feature branch so that its base becomes the tip of main, effectively moving all its commits after every commit on main. This operation would incorporate all commits from main, not just the one desired, and can rewrite public history, causing coordination problems with teammates. Therefore it does not satisfy the need to apply only a single commit.

**Option:** Cherry-pick the specific commit from main onto the feature branch using `git cherry-pick <commit‑sha>`. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Cherry-picking copies the changes introduced by the specified commit and creates a new commit on the current branch, leaving the rest of the main branch untouched. It lets you apply exactly one commit without pulling in unrelated history, which matches the requirement perfectly.

**Option:** Reset the feature branch to the commit from main with `git reset --hard <commit‑sha>`. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Resetting the branch to a commit from main discards all commits that were on the feature branch after that point, effectively losing work. It also moves the branch pointer, not copying the commit, which is not what is wanted when you simply need to bring one change over while preserving existing work. Hence this approach is incorrect.

**Option:** Pull the latest changes from main into the feature branch using `git pull origin main`. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** A pull combines a fetch and a merge, bringing all new commits from main into the feature branch. Like a plain merge, it adds the entire set of changes, not just the single commit of interest. This over‑includes changes and therefore does not meet the requirement.

**Option:** Create a new branch from the main commit and then merge it back into the feature branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While this could eventually bring the desired commit into the feature branch, it introduces an extra temporary branch and still requires a merge, which brings in all commits reachable from that new branch. The added complexity and over‑inclusion of history make it a suboptimal solution compared to cherry‑pick.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of how to bring an individual commit from one branch into another without merging full branch histories. The appropriate Git command for this scenario is `git cherry-pick`, which copies the changes introduced by a specific commit onto the current branch, preserving existing work and avoiding unrelated changes. Common misconceptions include using merge or rebase, which both propagate the entire commit series from the source branch, leading to unnecessary integration work. Reset and pull also misapply the concept: reset discards work, and pull merges all changes. Best practice is to use cherry-pick for isolated changes, and to ensure the commit is clean (no conflicts) before applying it to avoid later merge complications.

[Back to Question](#question-75)

### Question 76 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Create a new integration branch off the current production commit, merge both developers’ feature branches into it, resolve the conflicts manually, run the full test suite, and then merge the integration branch back into production.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Automatically accept the incoming changes using the 'theirs' strategy (git merge -X theirs) and discard the current production version of the conflicting files. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While the 'theirs' strategy forces acceptance of the incoming changes, it does so without reviewing the impact on production code, which can introduce bugs or regressions. Blindly overwriting production files bypasses essential code review and testing, potentially breaking the live system.

**Option:** Abort the merge, reset the production branch to the previous commit, and force‑push the other developer’s branch, effectively overwriting the production history. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Force‑pushing rewrites history on a critical production branch, which can confuse other collaborators and break CI/CD pipelines that rely on stable commit hashes. Overwriting production history also discards any unrelated changes that may have been safely deployed, increasing risk.

**Option:** Manually edit the conflicted files, resolve the differences, commit the merge, and then run the test suite before pushing the result to production. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is partially correct but incomplete. Manually resolving conflicts is necessary, but doing it directly on the production branch without isolation can expose the live environment to partially resolved code if tests fail. Best practice is to resolve conflicts in a separate branch where testing can be performed safely before merging back.

**Option:** Use the 'ours' merge strategy to keep the production branch’s version unchanged and ignore the conflicting changes from the feature branches. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The 'ours' strategy discards the incoming changes entirely, meaning the new feature work would be lost. Ignoring valid contributions defeats collaborative development and can cause duplicated effort or missed functionality.

**Option:** Delete the production branch, recreate it from the other developer’s branch, and push it as the new production line. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Deleting and recreating a production branch eliminates the audit trail and can unintentionally drop other critical changes. Such a drastic action should never be taken to resolve a simple merge conflict.

**Option:** Create a new integration branch off the current production commit, merge both developers’ feature branches into it, resolve the conflicts manually, run the full test suite, and then merge the integration branch back into production. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. By isolating conflict resolution in an integration branch, you protect the stable production branch from partial or faulty changes. After manual resolution, running the complete test suite ensures that the merged code works as expected before it is promoted to production, aligning with industry best practices for safe deployments.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of safe merge‑conflict resolution on a critical production branch. The optimal approach is to isolate the conflict in a temporary integration branch, manually resolve the differences, and thoroughly test before merging back, as described in option 6. Common misconceptions include using aggressive merge strategies like 'theirs' or 'ours' without review, force‑pushing, or directly committing fixes on production, all of which risk stability and auditability. Effective Dev Ops practice emphasizes preserving production integrity, maintaining clear history, and validating changes through testing. Remember to always resolve conflicts in a separate branch, involve relevant developers if needed, and run automated tests before promoting to production.

### Question 77 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** First pull the latest main into the feature branch, resolve the conflicts locally, commit the resolution, run tests, and then merge the feature branch into main via a pull request.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Abort the merge, delete the feature branch, and recreate it from the updated main branch, then push. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Deleting the feature branch discards all work that has been done on that branch, which is rarely desirable. In a real‑world scenario a developer would lose code, documentation, and history, requiring the effort to re‑implement the feature from scratch.

**Option:** Force push the feature branch over main using git push --force, overwriting the main branch with the feature branch's history. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This answer is also incorrect. Using --force on the main branch can erase other collaborators' commits, break the repository history, and cause downstream systems to fail. Force‑pushing in shared branches is considered a dangerous practice and is discouraged by most teams.

**Option:** First pull the latest main into the feature branch, resolve the conflicts locally, commit the resolution, run tests, and then merge the feature branch into main via a pull request. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This is the correct approach. By integrating the newest main into the feature branch first, the engineer can resolve conflicts in an isolated environment, verify that the combined code works with existing tests, and then submit a clean PR for review. This preserves history, maintains collaboration integrity, and minimizes the risk of introducing bugs into the main branch.

**Option:** Use git merge --strategy=ours when merging, which automatically keeps the feature branch's changes and discards main's conflicting changes. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. The 'ours' strategy unilaterally prefers the current branch's changes, potentially discarding important updates made on main. In production environments this can lead to missing bug fixes or security patches that were present in the main branch.

**Option:** Accept the Git Hub web UI's 'Resolve conflicts' tool without reviewing the changes, then complete the merge. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This answer is incorrect. Resolving conflicts without reviewing the diff can introduce subtle bugs, because the engineer may unintentionally keep or discard code that affects functionality. Best practice is to manually examine each conflict and run automated tests before completing the merge.

**Option:** Rebase the feature branch onto main, resolve any rebasing conflicts, then fast‑forward merge the feature branch into main. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** While rebasing can produce a linear history, it rewrites commit hashes and can cause problems for other collaborators who have already based work on the original feature branch. In a team setting, merging after conflict resolution is generally safer, making this option less optimal than the recommended local conflict resolution followed by a PR. Additionally, fast‑forward merges eliminate the merge commit that documents the integration point.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests the candidate's understanding of proper conflict resolution when integrating a feature branch into a protected main branch. The best practice is to pull the latest main into the feature branch, resolve conflicts locally, verify the combined code with testing, and then merge via a pull request, as described in option 3. Common misconceptions include deleting branches, force‑pushing, using aggressive merge strategies like 'ours', or relying on UI tools without review; each of these can lead to loss of work, broken history, or hidden bugs. Rebasing, while useful for a clean history, changes commit IDs and can disrupt collaboration, making it a less suitable default in shared environments. Teams should always prioritize safety, traceability, and verification before merging to main.

### Question 78 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Create a branch protection rule that enables "Require pull request reviews before merging" and sets "Required approving reviews" to 2.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Enable branch protection with "Require pull request reviews before merging" and set "Required approving reviews" to 1. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because it only mandates a single approving review. While it does enforce a review, the requirement stated in the scenario is for at least two reviewers. In practice, a PR could be merged after just one team member signs off, leaving the second review missing and potentially allowing defects to slip through.

**Option:** Add a CODEOWNERS file that lists all team members and enable "Require review from CODEOWNERS". [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This answer is incorrect. Requiring a review from a CODEOWNERS entry guarantees that at least one designated owner approves the change, but it does not enforce a count of two independent approvals. Teams often misuse CODEOWNERS as a proxy for multiple reviews, which can give a false sense of security when only one owner signs off.

**Option:** Create a branch protection rule that enables "Require pull request reviews before merging" and sets "Required approving reviews" to 2. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. The branch protection rule directly enforces the policy that every pull request must receive two separate approving reviews before it can be merged. In real-world scenarios, this prevents a single point of failure and encourages broader code ownership, reducing the likelihood of bugs reaching production.

**Option:** Configure a required status check for CI and enable "Require linear history". [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This answer is incorrect because required status checks and linear history address build integrity and commit ordering, not the number of human reviewers. While CI checks are essential, they do not substitute for peer review approvals. Relying solely on these settings would allow a PR to be merged after passing tests, even if only one person reviewed the code.

**Option:** Set "Require conversation resolution" on the protected branch without specifying a reviewer count. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Requiring conversation resolution forces reviewers to address all review comments, but it does not enforce how many reviewers must approve. A PR could be approved by a single reviewer who resolves all discussions, still failing to meet the two‑reviewer mandate.

**Option:** Write a Git Hub Actions workflow that automatically merges a PR after a single approving review. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This answer is incorrect. Automating a merge after only one approval directly contradicts the stipulated policy of two reviewers. Moreover, such automation can bypass manual checks and increase the risk of merging insufficiently vetted code, especially if the action misfires or the reviewer is not a subject‑matter expert.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of Git Hub branch protection rules, specifically how to enforce a minimum number of code‑review approvals. The correct configuration is to create a branch protection rule that both requires pull‑request reviews before merging and sets the required approving reviews count to two; this directly satisfies the policy. Common misconceptions include assuming that CODEOWNERS, required status checks, or conversation resolution alone control reviewer count—they address ownership, CI validation, and comment handling respectively, but not the number of approvals. Additionally, setting the required review count to one or using automation to merge after a single approval fails to meet the two‑reviewer requirement and can leave code quality unchecked. In practice, teams should combine branch protection with clear review policies to ensure robust peer review while still leveraging CI and automation for quality assurance.

### Question 79 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Enable a branch protection rule on the main branch that requires pull request reviews before merging.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Enable "Require signed commits" on the main branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Requiring signed commits only verifies the identity of the committer; it does not enforce that a human has reviewed the changes. In practice, a developer could sign and push a commit directly to main, bypassing any code‑review process.

**Option:** Turn on "Allow force pushes" for the main branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Allowing force pushes gives contributors the ability to rewrite history on the protected branch, which can undo or skip any review steps that were previously performed. Companies that need strict review policies usually disallow force pushes on main to preserve auditability.

**Option:** Enable a branch protection rule on the main branch that requires pull request reviews before merging. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A branch protection rule with the "Require pull request reviews before merging" setting blocks direct pushes and forces every change to go through a pull request that must be approved by at least one reviewer. Organizations such as large open‑source projects rely on this configuration to maintain code quality and accountability.

**Option:** Set a server‑side pre‑receive hook that blocks pushes lacking a GPG signature. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While a pre‑receive hook can reject unsigned commits, it does not mandate a peer review; developers could still push signed commits directly to main. Hooks are useful for enforcing policies like commit messages, but they are not a substitute for PR‑based review workflows.

**Option:** Activate "Require status checks to pass before merging" but do not enforce review. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Status checks ensure that automated tests or CI pipelines pass, but they do not guarantee a human has examined the code. A change could be merged automatically after tests succeed, even if no reviewer looked at the diff.

**Option:** Configure the repository's default branch to be a development branch and merge main via fast‑forward only. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Changing the default branch does not impose any review requirement; fast‑forward merges can still happen without a pull request. Without explicit protection rules, contributors could push directly to main, undermining the review process.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of Git Hub's branch protection features that enforce code review before changes reach the main branch. The correct configuration is to enable a branch protection rule that requires pull request reviews, which blocks direct pushes and mandates at least one approval. Common misconceptions include believing that signed commits, status checks, or pre‑receive hooks alone ensure review, but these mechanisms address authentication, CI status, or commit authenticity rather than human scrutiny. Allowing force pushes or relying on fast‑forward merges also defeats the purpose of a review gate. Best practice for large teams is to combine required reviews with status checks and disallow force pushes on protected branches to maintain both code quality and auditability.

### Question 80 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Enable a branch protection rule on the main branch that requires at least one approving pull‑request review before the merge can be completed.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Enable a branch protection rule on the main branch that requires at least one approving pull‑request review before the merge can be completed. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A branch protection rule with the "Require pull request reviews before merging" setting enforces that every change must be approved by a reviewer, preventing direct pushes or unreviewed merges. In practice, teams using this rule see higher code quality because no code reaches main without a second pair of eyes.

**Option:** Enable the "Require signed commits" setting on the main branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Requiring signed commits only verifies the author's identity; it does not enforce that another person reviews the changes. While useful for security, it would not stop a contributor from merging unreviewed code into main.

**Option:** Turn on "Allow force pushes" for the main branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Allowing force pushes actually bypasses the review process, letting anyone rewrite history on the protected branch. Enabling this would increase the risk of accidental loss of work or introduction of bugs without oversight.

**Option:** Set the repository visibility to private. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Making a repository private limits who can view it, but it does not impose any review workflow on merges. Private repos can still have unreviewed code merged if no branch protection is configured.

**Option:** Enable the "Auto‑merge" option for pull requests targeting the main branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Auto‑merge will automatically merge a pull request once all required status checks pass, but it does not create a requirement for a human review unless a review requirement is also set. Without the review rule, auto‑merge could bypass the intended review step.

**Option:** Configure a status check that only passes when CI builds succeed, without requiring a review. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While CI status checks ensure that code builds successfully, they do not guarantee that a peer has examined the logic, style, or potential defects. Relying solely on CI can let buggy or insecure code slip into main if no review gate exists.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of Git Hub branch protection rules that enforce code review before merging. The correct configuration is to enable a protection rule that requires at least one approving pull‑request review, which directly blocks merges without human approval. Options such as requiring signed commits, private visibility, or CI status checks are useful security or quality measures, but they do not by themselves enforce a review process. Allowing force pushes or enabling auto‑merge without a review requirement actually weakens the review gate. Best practice is to combine the review requirement with other checks (e. g., CI status) to ensure both quality and compliance before code reaches the main branch.

### Question 81 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Apply a branch protection rule on the main branch that requires a pull request review and passing status checks before merging.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Grant all team members 'admin' access to the repository. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because giving everyone admin rights removes any safeguards on the main branch. Admins can bypass branch protection rules, delete branches, and force‑push, which defeats the goal of maintaining control. In practice, a single mistaken admin push could rewrite history on main and disrupt the entire project.

**Option:** Disable branch protection and allow direct pushes to the main branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect as it removes the very mechanism that enforces review before changes reach main. Direct pushes let any contributor overwrite or introduce breaking changes without oversight. Real‑world teams that skip protection often experience unstable releases and higher rollback incidents.

**Option:** Apply a branch protection rule on the main branch that requires a pull request review and passing status checks before merging. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct because it lets anyone push to feature branches while ensuring main only changes via vetted pull requests. Requiring reviews and status checks enforces code quality, automated testing, and collaborative approval. Teams using this pattern keep the main branch stable, reducing production bugs and facilitating orderly releases.

**Option:** Set the repository to be public and rely on community contributions without any review process. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect; making a repo public invites external contributions, but without a review workflow the main branch can be polluted with untested code. Public open‑source projects typically enforce PR reviews precisely to avoid this risk. Applying no review process would compromise both security and code integrity for a private team project.

**Option:** Require that only the tech lead can push to any branch, while others can only read. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because it blocks the intended collaborative workflow. If contributors cannot push to their own branches, they must request the tech lead to create every feature branch, which creates a bottleneck and defeats the purpose of enabling contributions. Effective teams delegate branch creation rights and rely on PRs for control, not a single‑person push restriction.

**Option:** Enable "Allow force pushes" on the main branch to let anyone overwrite history. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect and contrary to the requirement of maintaining control. Allowing force pushes on main opens the door to accidental or malicious history rewrites, making it impossible to guarantee a stable baseline. Most professional workflows disable force pushes on protected branches to preserve auditability and continuity.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of how branch protection policies balance open contribution with safeguards on critical branches. The correct answer (option 3) implements a protection rule that forces all changes to main to go through pull‑request reviews and required status checks, preserving stability while still allowing developers to work freely on their own branches. Options 1, 2, 5, and 6 mistakenly grant excessive rights or remove safeguards, leading to potential chaos, loss of history, or bottlenecks. Option 4 misinterprets a public repository model and ignores the necessity of a review process for maintaining code quality. Best practice in professional Git workflows is to protect the main branch with mandatory reviews, CI checks, and to restrict direct pushes, ensuring a reliable production baseline while encouraging collaborative development.

### Question 82 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Create a branch protection rule on the main branch that (a) blocks direct pushes, (b) requires at least one approving pull‑request review, and (c) enforces status checks before merging.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Configure the main branch to allow force pushes but require a signed commit. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because allowing force pushes defeats the purpose of requiring review; anyone can overwrite history without oversight. Signed commits only verify author identity, not that the change has been examined by peers. In practice, a developer could force‑push unreviewed code, introducing bugs or security issues despite the signature.

**Option:** Set up a required status check that runs CI, but do not enforce any review policy. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While CI status checks catch build failures, they do not guarantee that a human has examined the code for logic errors, style, or security concerns. Teams relying solely on CI may merge code that passes tests but contains subtle defects that only a reviewer would spot.

**Option:** Create a branch protection rule on the main branch that (a) blocks direct pushes, (b) requires at least one approving pull‑request review, and (c) enforces status checks before merging. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Blocking direct pushes forces all changes to go through a pull request, and requiring an approving review ensures at least one teammate has examined the code. Adding required status checks guarantees that automated tests pass before the merge, providing a strong safety net that aligns with industry best practices for protected main branches.

**Option:** Enable the 'restrict who can push' setting for the main branch but leave pull‑request reviews optional. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because restricting push permissions alone does not compel code review; a trusted developer could still push directly if they have permission. Optional reviews are frequently bypassed in fast‑moving teams, leading to unvetted changes reaching production. Effective protection must combine both push restrictions and mandatory review enforcement.

**Option:** Use a merge strategy that automatically fast‑forwards any commit that passes CI, bypassing review. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Fast‑forward merges eliminate the explicit merge commit that documents review, and bypassing review means changes can be integrated as soon as tests pass, even if the code is defective or insecure. Real‑world teams avoid this pattern for critical branches like main, preferring pull‑request merges that preserve review metadata.

**Option:** Allow developers to merge their own pull requests after they have signed the Contributor License Agreement, without any additional checks. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Signing a CLA validates legal contribution rights but does not assure code quality or safety. Permitting self‑merges removes the peer‑review step, increasing the risk of bugs, regressions, or security vulnerabilities entering the main branch.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of Git Hub branch protection rules that enforce peer review before code reaches the main branch. The correct configuration combines three safeguards: blocking direct pushes, requiring at least one approving review, and mandating passing status checks such as CI. Many novices think that CI alone or push restrictions are sufficient, but without a mandatory review step unexamined code can still be merged. Conversely, allowing only push restrictions or self‑merges overlooks the collaborative inspection that catches logical errors and security flaws. Best practice is to enable a comprehensive branch protection rule that enforces reviews, tests, and prevents direct changes, ensuring a reliable and auditable workflow.

### Question 83 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answers:**
- Create a branch protection rule that requires an approving pull‑request review before merging.
- Set up a required status check that the CI build must pass before the pull request can be merged.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Disable branch protection for the main branch to allow immediate merges. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because turning off branch protection removes any enforcement of review or CI checks. Without protection, developers can push directly to main, bypassing the pull‑request workflow entirely. In real projects this often leads to bugs reaching production and makes rollbacks more frequent.

**Option:** Create a branch protection rule that requires an approving pull‑request review before merging. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. A branch protection rule can be configured to block merges to main until at least one reviewer has approved the pull request, guaranteeing that human eyes have examined the changes. Teams that enforce this see higher code quality and fewer regression incidents because every change is vetted before it hits the main branch.

**Option:** Configure the repository to allow maintainers to bypass pull‑request reviews. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Allowing maintainers to skip the review requirement defeats the purpose of a review process and creates a privileged path that can be abused or used accidentally. Organizations that rely on strict governance usually disable this bypass to keep the audit trail consistent.

**Option:** Set up a required status check that the CI build must pass before the pull request can be merged. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. Required status checks make Git Hub reject a merge until the designated CI workflow finishes successfully, ensuring that tests, linting, and other automated validations have cleared. In practice, this prevents broken code from being merged and provides immediate feedback to developers when their changes fail the pipeline.

**Option:** Enable required pull‑request reviewers (code owners) so that specific team members must approve changes. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect as a standalone measure because code owners are optional and only apply if you have defined a CODEOWNERS file. Merely enabling the feature does not force a review unless the owners are explicitly required, and it does not guarantee that the CI checks have passed. Relying solely on code owners can give a false sense of security if the protection rules are not also set.

**Option:** Enable automatic merging of pull requests after a single commit without any review. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect because automatic merging without review contradicts the requirement to have changes examined before they reach main. While auto‑merge can be useful for trivial changes, using it for feature work removes the gate that catches bugs and design issues. Deployments that skip review often suffer from undetected defects that increase incident response time.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of Git Hub branch protection mechanisms that enforce code review and CI validation before code reaches the main branch. Correct answers involve configuring a protection rule that mandates an approving pull‑request review and setting required status checks so that the CI pipeline must succeed. Common misconceptions include thinking that disabling protection or allowing maintainers to bypass reviews still maintains quality, or assuming that code‑owner settings alone are sufficient without explicit review requirements. In practice, organizations combine these controls to create a robust gating strategy that catches both human errors and automated test failures. Following these best practices helps maintain a stable main branch and reduces the risk of production incidents.

### Question 84 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** Enable branch protection rules on the main branch that require signed commits and that a CI job (e. g., a verification workflow) passes before the branch can be merged or pushed.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** Require that every pull request be merged with the “merge commit” option disabled, forcing a fast‑forward only workflow. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option describes a merge strategy that controls how history looks, but it does not enforce any verification of the commit contents. Fast‑forward merges simply move the branch pointer; they do not run tests, check signatures, or guarantee that code has been approved. Consequently, relying on this setting would leave the production branch vulnerable to unverified changes.

**Option:** Configure a pre‑receive hook on the central repository that automatically signs each incoming commit, ensuring they are verified. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Pre‑receive hooks can reject commits that do not meet criteria, but they cannot retroactively sign commits; signatures must be created by the author before the push. Attempting to add a signature in a server‑side hook would break the commit hash, invalidating the object. Therefore, this statement is technically inaccurate and would not achieve the intended verification.

**Option:** Enable branch protection rules on the main branch that require signed commits and that a CI job (e. g., a verification workflow) passes before the branch can be merged or pushed. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** Branch protection with required signed commits and required status checks is the recommended way to guarantee that only verified code reaches production. Git Hub will block pushes or merges that lack a valid GPG/SSH signature and will also enforce that a configured CI workflow completes successfully. This ensures that every change has both developer accountability and automated verification before it can be deployed.

**Option:** Set up a scheduled Git Hub Action that scans the repository nightly and retroactively adds a ‘verified’ label to any commit that passed tests. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Adding a label after the fact does not prevent unverified commits from being merged or deployed earlier in the day. The pipeline would still have to process potentially unsafe code before the nightly scan runs. Hence, this approach does not satisfy the requirement that verification happen before deployment.

**Option:** Allow direct pushes to the production branch and rely on the deployment pipeline’s runtime checks to block unverified code. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Direct pushes bypass any pre‑merge checks such as required status checks or signed‑commit enforcement, placing the burden on runtime checks that occur after code has already entered the production branch. This defeats the purpose of verifying commits before they are deployed and can lead to race conditions or missed failures. Best practice is to prevent the push itself rather than trying to catch problems later.

**Option:** Use Git tags marked as ‘verified’ and configure the pipeline to deploy only tagged commits, assuming tags guarantee verification. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** Tags are simply pointers to commits and carry no intrinsic verification data; anyone can create a tag named ‘verified’ without running tests or signing. Deploying based solely on tag names provides a false sense of security and can allow unverified code to be released if a tag is applied incorrectly. Proper verification must be enforced at the commit or branch level, not through tag naming conventions.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests knowledge of how to enforce commit verification in a CI/CD workflow, specifically using Git Hub's branch protection features. Requiring signed commits and mandatory status checks ensures that code cannot be merged or pushed to the protected branch unless it passes automated tests and bears a valid developer signature. Options 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 each reflect common misunderstandings: they either address unrelated Git mechanics, describe technically impossible actions, rely on retroactive labeling, or trust inadequate mechanisms like tags. In real‑world pipelines, the safest practice is to block unverified changes at the point of integration, not after they have reached production. By configuring branch protection with required checks, teams achieve both accountability and automated quality assurance before deployment.

### Question 85 Explanation

::: correctbox

**Correct Answer:** The remote branch has new commits that the local branch does not contain, causing a divergence.

:::

#### [Explanations for all options:]{.underline}

**Option:** The remote repository is behind the local branch, so Git refuses the push. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. A non-fast-forward error occurs when the remote branch is *ahead* of the local branch, not when it is behind. If the remote were behind, Git would simply fast‑forward the remote to match the local, and no error would be raised.

**Option:** The developer lacks push permissions on the remote repository. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Permission problems produce authentication or "permission denied" messages, not a non‑fast‑forward error. The non‑fast‑forward condition is about commit history, not access rights.

**Option:** The remote branch has new commits that the local branch does not contain, causing a divergence. [**(Correct)**]{.correct-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is correct. When the remote contains commits unknown to the local repository, a simple push would discard those remote commits, so Git blocks the operation with a non‑fast‑forward error. The developer must first integrate the remote changes via `git pull --rebase` or `git fetch` followed by a merge before pushing again.

**Option:** The . gitignore file prevents the new changes from being tracked, leading to the error. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. . gitignore only tells Git which files to ignore; it does not influence the history‑based checks that produce a non‑fast‑forward error. Ignored files simply are not staged, and the push would succeed if the commit history were compatible.

**Option:** A server‑side pre‑receive hook rejects pushes that contain merge commits. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. While hooks can reject pushes, they emit custom error messages defined by the repository administrator. A standard non‑fast‑forward error is generated by Git itself when the histories diverge, not by a hook rejecting merge commits.

**Option:** The developer is attempting to push a lightweight tag instead of a branch. [**(Incorrect)**]{.incorrect-text}

> **Explanation:** This option is incorrect. Pushing a tag does not generate a non‑fast‑forward error because tags are not part of branch history. If a tag already exists on the remote, Git would either update it (if forced) or report a different message, not the non‑fast‑forward warning.

#### [Overall Explanation:]{.underline}

The question tests understanding of why Git reports a non‑fast‑forward error during a push. This error occurs when the remote branch has commits that the local branch does not, meaning the histories have diverged and a simple fast‑forward update is impossible. The correct remedy is to incorporate the remote changes first, typically by pulling (with merge or rebase) or fetching and manually merging. Common misconceptions include blaming permission issues, . gitignore settings, or server hooks, but those produce different error messages. Best practice is to regularly synchronize with the remote (`git pull --rebase`) before pushing, and to examine `git status` and `git log --oneline origin/branch.. branch` to see the divergence.
